headline: The Navajo Nation elected its first woman president.
summary: Crystalyne Curley won the Navajo Nation's presidency Tuesday, the first woman to hold it since the tribal government was set up a century ago. The same night Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the US Senate, and Deb Haaland the first to be a governor, in New Mexico. The Seneca Nation picked a woman president too.

cover_question.q: Why did it take this long?

cover_answer: Men have run it since it was set up a century ago.
table_question: Does the first person to do something have to be twice as good?

5-7.script: A woman named Crystalyne Curley was just picked to lead the Navajo Nation, whose land spreads across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. In third grade she went on a field trip, watched the leaders argue, and decided that was where she wanted to be. No woman had ever had the job. Now one does.
5-7.why: The field trip is the anchor: a kid near their age deciding what she wanted. At seven one girl and one wish is the whole story, and 'first woman' is a fact they can hold.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them one girl on a field trip who decided where she wanted to be and got there. 'First woman' is a fact they can hold without the century behind it. Expect "is she the boss of everyone?" She leads the Navajo government from January, with Chris Deschene as her deputy.

8-12.script: The Navajo Nation's government was set up a century ago, and every president since has been a man. Some Navajo people say tradition means the top job is for men. Crystalyne Curley ran anyway and won, narrowly. Think of a club rule nobody ever wrote down, until someone asks why.
8-12.why: An unwritten rule, a challenger, a result: a chain they follow at ten.
8-12.why_long: At this age they are working out rules and whether adults apply them fairly, so the script hands over a chain: a rule nobody wrote down, a candidate who ran anyway and won narrowly. The club rule nobody wrote down is one they know. Expect "so was the rule wrong?" Some Navajo people still say tradition bars it. The voters said otherwise.

13-17.script: Only four Native Americans have been US senators in 230 years, all men. Why? Peggy Flanagan is now the first Native woman senator, Deb Haaland the first Native woman governor, and Crystalyne Curley the first woman to lead the Navajo Nation. Second: is a first a win, or a measure of the wait?
13-17.why: Three firsts and a 230-year wait are both true. At 15 they can weigh both.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: three firsts in one night, and a Senate that seated four Native people in 230 years, all men. The script sets the win against the wait and asks which is the story. Expect "why does it matter what they are?" Curley's answer: a higher standard, and twice the work.

5-7.q: Why is it a big deal that she's a girl?
5-7.a: No woman had ever led the Navajo Nation before. She's the first.

8-12.q: Why hadn't a woman won before?
8-12.a: Some say Navajo tradition keeps the top job for men. Voters disagreed.

8-12.q: Did she win by a lot?
8-12.a: No. Narrowly, the article says, and the count is still unofficial.

13-17.q: Why did it take this long?
13-17.a: A century of men in the Navajo job. Four Native senators, all men.

13-17.q: Does being first make the job harder?
13-17.a: She thinks so. 'We have to work twice or triple as hard,' she said.
